question: ATS 7.13.D gives which ground-resistance screens, unless the owner specifies otherwise?
choices: 25 Ω for substations and 5 Ω point-to-point
5 Ω for large commercial or industrial systems, 1 Ω or less for generating or transmission stations, and investigate point-to-point above 0.5 Ω
0.5 Ω for every rod, with no point-to-point test
100 Ω, corrected for temperature
explanation: 7.13.D.2 is 5 ohms and 1 ohm, citing IEEE 142. 7.13.D.3 is 0.5 ohm point-to-point. The NEC 25-ohm supplemental-rod rule is a different document and does not replace these.

question: ATS 7.13.B.2 tells you to perform the electrode resistance test:
choices: With a megohmmeter at 1000 V
By fall-of-potential or an alternative, in accordance with IEEE 81
By the formula 100 divided by length in feet
Only with a clamp-on meter, probes forbidden
explanation: The paragraph names fall-of-potential or an alternative, and it names IEEE 81. It does not put a 62% spacing in the NETA sentence. The 100/length formula is busway insulation resistance, not a ground rod.

question: A zero-sequence ground-fault sensor on a solidly grounded service should have:
choices: All phase conductors and the neutral through the sensor in the same direction, and no equipment-grounding conductor through it
Only the equipment-grounding conductor through the sensor
Each phase through its own window in opposite directions
The neutral stopped on the load side of the sensor so it cannot be seen
explanation: ATS 7.14 visual checks: phases and neutral pass through in the same direction; grounding conductors do not. The ground bond itself lands on the source side of the sensor and of the neutral disconnect.

question: ATS 7.14 wants the ground connection:
choices: On the load side of the ground-fault sensor so the sensor sees neutral current
On the source side of the neutral disconnect link and on the source side of any ground-fault sensor
Removed entirely on a solidly grounded service
Run through the zero-sequence window together with the phases
explanation: Source side of the neutral disconnect and source side of the sensor. A ground on the load side of a zero-sequence sensor, or an equipment ground passed through the window, changes what the relay sees. Put the neutral link back after the neutral-to-ground insulation test.

question: A fall-of-potential test is still sloping at every probe position. The useful next step is:
choices: Average the slope and publish it
Move the current probe farther out until a flat section appears
Switch to a megohmmeter at 1000 V
Report 25 Ω because that is the NEC cap
explanation: If the fall-of-potential curve never flattens, the current probe is still inside the electrode's resistance area. Move it farther out until a flat section appears, and set the potential probe on that flat part. ATS-2025 7.13.B.2 names fall-of-potential for this test. The 25 Ω figure is a different rule and is not this test's target.

question: A clamp-on ground tester on a single rod whose bonding has been lifted will:
choices: Read the true electrode resistance
Lack a return path, so the reading is not the rod’s resistance
Match a fall-of-potential test within 1%
Satisfy ATS 7.13 by itself
explanation: A clamp-on looks at a loop. With the bond open there is no loop, and the number is not the electrode's resistance to earth. ATS 7.13.D.2 is where the 5 Ω and 1 Ω comparison values sit. Fall-of-potential is the method 7.13.B.2 names.
reference: Engineering fundamentals (clamp-on ground tester); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.13.B.2 and 7.13.D.2

question: A zero-sequence sensor was installed with one phase left outside the window. ATS 7.14’s check that fails is:
choices: All phase conductors and the neutral pass through in the same direction
The ground rod is under 5 Ω
The neutral is unbonded
Watts-loss of the arrester
explanation: Leaving a phase outside the window makes normal current look like residual. 7.14 requires every phase and the neutral through the sensor in the same direction, and it forbids the equipment ground in that window.

question: The fall-of-potential test named in ATS 7.13 is run by:
choices: A probe spacing in feet printed in that NETA paragraph
IEEE 81, or another method that section allows
A megohmmeter
Passing any reading at or under 25 ohms
explanation: ATS 7.13.B.2 points this test at IEEE 81 or at another method that section allows. It does not print a probe spacing of its own. A megohmmeter does not make this measurement, and 25 ohms is a different rule.

question: Temporary grounds go on only after the absence-of-voltage test because:
choices: Grounds prove the circuit is dead
A ground on a live phase is a fault; 1910.333 and 70E both want the test first
The ground set replaces the lock
IEEE 81 requires grounds before the test
explanation: You do not ground a circuit you have not proved dead. 1910.333 has the qualified person test first. NFPA 70E-2024 120.6 puts the voltage test at step 7 and the grounds, when they are required, at step 8.

question: A transformer neutral grounding impedance device is judged by ATS 7.2.2.D.18 against:
choices: The manufacturer’s published data
Table 100.11
Five ohms, always
The cable-shield ohms-per-foot rule
explanation: The reactor or resistor has its own rating. ATS says to compare the measured value with what the manufacturer published. The 5-ohm ground-grid figure and the machine insulation table are different tests.

question: The ATS test for the resistance of the main grounding electrode is:
choices: Point-to-point only
Fall-of-potential, or an alternative in accordance with IEEE 81
A megohmmeter from the rod to the fence
The busway 100-divided-by-length formula
explanation: Fall-of-potential is the electrode test. Point-to-point is the bonding check, and readings above 0.5 ohm are investigated. A megohmmeter does not measure soil resistance. The 62 percent spacing is IEEE 81 practice, not a number ATS prints.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 electrical testing of grounding and bonding, conditions 1, 2, and 3, is:
choices: 60, 36, and 36 months
12, 12, and 6 months, which is the visual row
60, 36, and 12 months, the ordinary standard row
3, 3, and 1 month
explanation: Visual inspection of grounding and bonding is 12, 12, and 6 months. Electrical testing is 60, 36, and 36 months. The chapter lists fall-of-potential, point-to-point bonding, and connection resistance, and it does not print a universal ohm limit for the earth electrode.

question: Which test is on the NFPA 70B-2026 Table 20.3.5 grounding list?
choices: Fall-of-potential on a ground rod, point-to-point bonding, and connection resistance
A transformer turns-ratio test
Inverse-time trip at 300 percent
Specific gravity of 10 percent of the cells
explanation: The grounding table also includes substation-grid integrity and voltage or current on grounding conductors. It does not publish one ohm value that every electrode must hit. Manufacturer or project limits still govern the number.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 chapter 20 does not give one earth-resistance number that every electrode must meet. The tests it does list include:
choices: Fall-of-potential, point-to-point bonding, and connection resistance
A required maximum of 1 ohm for every site
Inverse-time trip at 300 percent
Oil acidity
explanation: The chapter also lists substation-grid integrity and voltage or current on grounding conductors. Connection resistance is still investigated when it exceeds the manufacturer’s maximum, under the fundamental bolted-joint rule. The ohm value of the electrode, when someone has set one, comes from the project or from the NETA paragraph you are applying, not from a blank in this chapter.

question: Fall-of-potential on a single driven rod, probes in a straight line on the same side. The current probe is 100 ft from the rod. Using the 62% rule, the potential probe goes about:
choices: 62 ft from the rod
38 ft from the rod
50 ft from the rod, halfway
100 ft from the rod, next to the current probe
explanation: The 62% rule puts the potential probe at roughly 0.618 of the rod-to-current-probe distance, measured from the electrode under test, when both probes are on the same side. 0.62 × 100 ft is about 62 ft. Measuring from the current probe end (38 ft) is the classic mix-up.

question: On an ATS 7.13 fall-of-potential test, the 62% probe position gives a trustworthy reading only when:
choices: The soil is fairly uniform, the probes are far enough out to act like hemispheres, and the electrode has no outside ground connections
The current probe is within one rod length of the electrode
The electrode stays bonded to the utility neutral during the test
The test is run at exactly 60 Hz so the reading matches power frequency
explanation: The 62% figure comes from theory for a small electrode in uniform soil with remote probes. Layered soil, short spacing, or a ground that is still tied to other grounds (neutrals, shields, other grids) all move the correct probe spot, so the rule stops applying and you fall back on plotting a curve. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.13.B.2; ref. IEEE 81-2012, 8.2.2.4.1.

question: Setting up an ATS 7.13 fall-of-potential test, how far from the electrode under test does the current probe typically go?
choices: Equal to the depth of the rod
62% of the electrode's largest dimension
About five times the largest dimension of the electrode
A fixed 10 ft, whatever the electrode size
explanation: The current probe has to be far enough out that the electrode's and probe's resistance zones do not overlap. The guide's typical figure is at least five times the electrode's largest dimension, which is why a large grid needs very long leads.

question: A Wenner four-point soil test uses equal probe spacing a = 3 m, probes driven shallow (no deeper than a tenth of the spacing). The meter reads R = 5 Ω. Apparent resistivity is about:
choices: 94 Ω·m
15 Ω·m
47 Ω·m
explanation: With shallow probes the Wenner formula reduces to ρ = 2πaR. 2 × 3.1416 × 3 m × 5 Ω ≈ 94 Ω·m. Leaving out the 2 gives 47, and leaving out π gives roughly 30. The result is the average resistivity to a depth of about a.

question: You're asked to check a substation ground grid, which has many paths to earth, with a clamp-on (stakeless) ground tester. What's the problem?
choices: Clamp-on is the preferred method for substation grids because no probes are needed
The clamp-on method does not apply to a multiply connected system like a substation grid, so use fall-of-potential or another staked method
Clamp-on works on a grid if you clamp the largest down conductor
Clamp-on reads the grid correctly as long as the jaws are clean
explanation: A clamp-on meter assumes everything except the electrode under test is close to zero ohms, so it only works on one electrode tied to a low-impedance multigrounded neutral or shield. The guide lists substation grids and multiconnected poles or structures as places where the method does not apply.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.13.B.2; ref. IEEE 81-2012, 8.2.2.5 item d)

question: You are testing a large grid expected to read below 1 Ω, and the current and potential leads run side by side for hundreds of feet. What is the concern, and how do you fix it?
choices: Lead resistance adds to the reading. Use a thicker potential lead
Parallel leads cancel the test current. Twist the leads together
There is no concern below 1 Ω, because coupling only matters above 10 Ω
Mutual coupling from the current lead adds voltage to the potential lead. Separate the leads or cross them at right angles
explanation: Ac coupling between parallel leads puts an error voltage on the potential circuit. It does not matter much at 10 Ω and up, but it almost always matters at 1 Ω or less, which is exactly where big grids land. Route the leads apart, or at 90° where they must cross.

question: The ground tester flags low test current because the current probe's own resistance is too high in dry soil. What's the right fix?
choices: Mix salt into the water, since salt rather than moisture is what lowers probe resistance
Lower the probe resistance: drive it deeper, wet the soil around it, or add rods in parallel spaced at least their buried length apart
Move the potential probe closer to the electrode under test
Switch the tester to a higher voltage, since test voltage above 50 V carries no extra hazard
explanation: The usual cure is to lower the current-electrode resistance. The guide notes that moisture does the work and salt adds very little. Higher-voltage instruments are possible, but above 50 V the leads and probes become a shock hazard to people.

question: Three-point (triangulation) method on a rod: rod to probe 2 reads 30 Ω, rod to probe 3 reads 34 Ω, probe 2 to probe 3 reads 40 Ω. The rod resistance is:
explanation: Each reading is the sum of two electrode resistances, so solving the three equations gives r1 = (r12 + r13 − r23) / 2 = (30 + 34 − 40) / 2 = 12 Ω. If the electrodes are too close together, mutual resistance can produce nonsense such as zero or negative answers.

question: You want to test the ground lead of a surge arrester whose line terminal is still connected to an energized line. What's the rule?
choices: Never disconnect the arrester ground while the line terminal is energized, because the arrester base can rise toward line potential
Lift the ground lead briefly, since arresters carry no current at normal voltage
Disconnect the ground lead only during dry weather
Disconnect the ground lead, but wear Class 0 gloves
explanation: An arrester with its ground removed and its top still on the line can put the base near line voltage. The guide says the ground lead can be tested only with suitable precautions, and never lifted while the primary is connected to an energized line.

question: A fall-of-potential reading from one ground riser comes in far higher than the design value. A sensible first step is:
choices: Accept the reading, since one riser represents the whole grid
Move the potential probe to 90% of the current-probe distance
Divide the reading by the number of risers
Suspect a poor connection from that riser to the grid and repeat the test from other points on the grid
explanation: The test measures from the point you clip to, out to remote earth. If that conductor is poorly bonded to the grid, the reading jumps. Repeat from other risers. Large differences between them point to grid damage, and a grid integrity (continuity) test is the next step. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.13.B.2; ref. IEEE 81-2012, 8.2.2.4.1.

question: On a high-resistance grounded system, the first line-to-ground fault is usually handled by:
choices: Instantaneous tripping of the main breaker
Letting several thousand amps flow so the feeder breaker clears it
Alarming and continuing to run, with fault current typically held to about 10 A or less
Blowing the neutral fuse
explanation: High-resistance grounding keeps ground-fault current low enough to flow for a long time, so protection is normally detection and alarm, not immediate trip. That is why the resistor needs a continuous rating, and why the fault still has to be found and cleared.

question: A 4160 V wye system is to be low-resistance grounded with ground-fault current limited to 400 A. Ignoring system impedance, the neutral resistor is about:
explanation: Size the resistor from the line-to-neutral voltage: R = Vln / Ig. 4160 / √3 ≈ 2402 V, and 2402 / 400 ≈ 6.0 Ω. Using the line-to-line voltage gives 10.4 Ω, which lets less current flow than intended.

question: On an ungrounded three-phase system, phase C faults solidly to ground. The two healthy phases now sit at about what voltage to ground?
choices: Zero
Half the line-to-neutral voltage
Unchanged at line-to-neutral voltage
Line-to-line voltage, √3 times their normal line-to-neutral voltage
explanation: With one phase at ground, the system's capacitive neutral shifts, and the other two phases see full line-to-line voltage to ground. The total charging current that flows into the fault is three times the normal per-phase value.

question: A single driven rod reads 22 Ω, and someone says the plant ground system is fine because it's under the NEC 25 Ω figure. Is that right?
choices: Correct: 25 Ω is the recommended value for industrial substations
Correct, as long as the reading was taken in dry season
The NEC figure applies only to generating stations
The 25 Ω value only decides whether a single electrode needs a supplemental electrode. It is not a satisfactory system value
explanation: The Green Book describes 1 Ω to 5 Ω as generally suitable for industrial plant substations and large commercial buildings, and below 1 Ω for large substations and generating stations. The NEC 25 Ω number is only a trigger for adding a second electrode.

question: When a high-resistance grounding resistor is sized, its let-through current is chosen to be:
choices: Well below the charging current, so the fault current stays as small as possible
Equal to the three-phase bolted fault current
Large enough to trip the feeder instantaneous element
Equal to or slightly greater than the system's total capacitive charging current
explanation: Setting the resistor current at or a little above the total charging current (3Ico) is what controls transient overvoltage from arcing or restriking ground faults. A resistor that lets through less than the charging current loses that benefit. The guide also cautions against high-resistance grounding where ground-fault current would exceed about 10 A.

question: A new industrial plant substation's ground system measures 3 Ω. Against common industry guidance, that is:
choices: Too high; every system must be under 1 Ω
In the 1 to 5 Ω range generally found suitable for industrial plant substations and large commercial buildings
Only acceptable if under the 25 Ω single-electrode value
Not something a resistance value can judge
explanation: Grounding guidance puts 1 to 5 Ω as generally suitable for industrial plant substations, buildings, and large commercial sites. Under 1 Ω is for large substations, transmission lines, and generating stations. ATS uses the same 5 Ω figure when the owner gives no other value. Source: IEEE 142-2007, 4.1.3; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.13.D.2.

question: To lower a high-reading electrode, a contractor proposes adding rods 4 ft apart around the existing rod. The better practice is:
choices: Fine; closer is better
Space them farther apart; spacings under about 3 m (10 ft) tend not to use the material economically
Bond them with insulated wire only
Use one shorter rod instead
explanation: Rods placed close together share the same soil and add little. Grounding guidance says spacings under about 3 m (10 ft) may not be the most economical use of material, and deeper rods often help because soil resistivity usually falls with depth. Source: IEEE 142-2007, 4.2 and 4.2.2.

question: An electrode was improved years ago by chemically treating the soil, and its resistance has been rising at each test since. What is the likely reason?
choices: Chemical treatment is not permanent and has to be replenished
The rod has grown longer
Treatment makes soil resistivity rise over time by design
The test method changed
explanation: Chemical treatment can cut soil resistivity a great deal, but it washes out and must be renewed on a maintenance schedule. It can also speed corrosion of the electrode. Periodic tests are how you see the rise. Source: IEEE 142-2007, 4.1.7 and 4.4.3.

question: A substation ground grid measures 0.4 Ω, and the study shows a maximum grid current of 5000 A for a ground fault. The ground potential rise is about:
explanation: Ground potential rise is the maximum grid current times the grid resistance: 5000 A × 0.4 Ω = 2000 V relative to remote earth. Source: IEEE 80-2013, 8.1 (definition of GPR).

question: When a step and touch voltage study uses the 70 kg body-weight criterion instead of 50 kg, where is that appropriate?
choices: Anywhere
Where the people exposed can be expected to average at least 70 kg, such as fenced switchyards closed to the public
Only outside the fence
Only for metal-to-metal touch
explanation: The 70 kg constant gives higher tolerable voltages. It is meant for places the public cannot reach, such as fenced or walled switchyards. For areas outside the fence, an assessment should decide whether the 50 kg criterion is needed. Source: IEEE 80-2013, 6.2 and its footnote.

question: Using IEEE 80-2013, find the tolerable touch voltage for a 50 kg person, fault clearing in 0.5 s, no surface layer, soil 100 Ω·m.
choices: About 189 V
About 164 V
About 133 V
About 271 V
explanation: Etouch50 = (1000 + 1.5·Cs·ρs) × 0.116 / √ts. With no surface layer, Cs = 1 and ρs = soil ρ. (1000 + 150) × 0.116 / 0.707 ≈ 189 V. Source: IEEE 80-2013, 8.4, Equation (32).

question: In IEEE 80-2013, what happens to the touch voltage limit for metal-to-metal contact, such as hand to a structure while standing on a grounded platform?
choices: It uses ρs = 0, so only the 1000 Ω body resistance limits current and the tolerable voltage is lowest
It doubles
It uses the step equation
It is ignored
explanation: For metal-to-metal contact, foot resistance drops out (ρs = 0), so the circuit is just the body's 1000 Ω. At 0.5 s and 50 kg, that's 1000 × 0.116 / 0.707 ≈ 164 V. Source: IEEE 80-2013, 7.1 and 8.4.

question: Dalziel's body-current equation in IEEE 80-2013 (IB = k/√ts) is valid over what range of shock durations?
choices: 0.001 s to 1 s
0.5 s to 10 s
Any duration
explanation: The equation is based on tests between 0.03 s and 3.0 s, so it isn't valid for very short or long durations. For 50 kg, k = 0.116, giving 116 mA at 1 s and 367 mA at 0.1 s. Source: IEEE 80-2013, 6.1.

question: Why does IEEE 80-2013 recommend a 0.08 m to 0.15 m layer of crushed rock or similar in a substation yard?
choices: To improve grid resistance
High-resistivity surface material adds foot resistance and cuts shock current, and it slows topsoil drying
To lower GPR
To protect conductors from frost
explanation: A high-resistivity layer increases the foot contact resistance in the step and touch equations (through Cs·ρs), reducing body current. It also slows moisture loss from topsoil in dry weather. It does not reduce the grid's resistance or GPR. Source: IEEE 80-2013, 7.4 and 12.5.
